topics.title: UNGA 81 Presidency
bullets: The United Nations General Assembly held a secret ballot on 2 June 2026 to elect its next President for the 81st session.
Two candidates are in the fray: Bangladesh's Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman (won) and Cyprus's Special Envoy for Multilateralism Andreas Kakouris.
This election is a crucial moment for the UN as it navigates global conflicts and prepares to select the next Secretary-General. What is the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA)?
The UNGA is the main deliberative, policymaking, and representative organ of the United Nations. Its first session was convened on 10 January 1946 at Central Hall in London.
It is the only UN body with universal representation, as all 193 Member States are represented in it.
It meets annually in New York, where heads of state gather for the high-level General Debate.
The UNGA approves the UN's regular and peacekeeping budgets and supports the work of its committees.
It also plays a key role in electing the non-permanent members of the Security Council and appointing the UN Secretary- General.
Decisions on important questions, such as peace and security or admitting new members, require a two-thirds majority.
The President of the General Assembly (PGA) is the chief presiding officer elected to serve a one-year term.
The PGA chairs meetings, rules on points of order, and guides the adoption of resolutions, carrying significant moral authority.
Recent presidents have used the platform to champion priorities such as UN reform, climate action, and the Sustainable Development Goals.
The 80th session of the UNGA was led by President Annalena Baerbock, the former foreign minister of Germany.
She is only the fifth woman to hold the post in the UN's 80-year history.
She set out her “Better Together” vision, calling for unity in the face of global crises, a theme that resonated throughout her tenure. The Election Process –
The presidency of the UNGA rotates among five regional groups: Africa, Asia-Pacific, Eastern Europe, Latin America, and Western Europe.
For the 81st session, the President will be elected from the Asia-Pacific Group.
This system ensures equitable geographical representation in the leadership of the General Assembly.
According to Rule 30 of the UN's Rules of Procedure, the election must be held at least three months before the new session opens.
In accordance with Rule 92, the election is held by secret ballot, and there are no formal nominations.
A candidate must secure a simple majority of the members present and voting to be declared the winner.
To ensure transparency, the UN holds informal interactive dialogues where candidates present their vision statements.
These dialogues allow member states, civil society organizations, and individuals to ask questions directly to the candidates.
The dialogues for the 81st session were convened on 13 May 2026 by the current President, Annalena Baerbock.
The PGA is expected to serve as a "full-time president" acting with strict impartiality to forge consensus on divisive issues.
The election for the UNGA President will be held just a day before the UN elects five new non-permanent members to the Security Council.
These members will serve two-year terms (2027-2028) on the 15- member body responsible for maintaining international peace and security.
The five outgoing non-permanent members (Denmark, Greece, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia) will be replaced on 1 January 2027.
Five other non-permanent members are Bahrain, Colombia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Latvia, and Liberia whose terms continue until January 1, 2028. The Two Candidates –
Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh is a veteran diplomat with over 30 years of experience within the United Nations system.
He has served as Bangladesh's National Security Adviser and was sworn in as Foreign Minister in February 2026.
He pledges to be a "full-time President" serving the interests of all member states without fear or favor.
Khalilur Rahman has framed his candidacy as carrying the "aspirations of developing countries" from the Global South.
His work has focused on development issues affecting Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and Small Island Developing States (SIDS).
This perspective is crucial as the UNGA addresses existential threats like sea-level rise and pandemic preparedness.
If elected, Rahman would be the second person from Bangladesh to head the UN General Assembly.
The first was Humayun Rasheed Choudhury, who served as President of the 41st session in 1986.
This bid comes over 40 years after Bangladesh last held the prestigious position.
Andreas Kakouris of Cyprus is a seasoned diplomat with over 40 years of experience, having served as ambassador to the US and the UK.
He began his career in New York in the 1980s, giving him deep institutional knowledge of the UN.
His vision, "Our Home, Our Future, Our Responsibility," stresses practical multilateralism and restoring trust in the UN.
Andreas Kakouris positions Cyprus, an EU member, as a natural bridge-builder between Europe and other regions.
His platform emphasizes ocean governance, climate resilience, and the inclusion of smaller delegations in decision-making.
He promises to bring greater transparency and a focus on delivering tangible results for people, particularly small and vulnerable states.
If elected, Kakouris would become the first Cypriot to head the UN General Assembly.
Cyprus positions itself as a natural bridge-builder between different blocs in the international community.
This represents a significant diplomatic achievement for Cyprus, a nation that has been a UN member since 1960.
Palestine had initially entered the race but withdrew its candidacy, paving the way for a direct contest between Bangladesh and Cyprus.
Bangladesh had announced its candidacy years earlier, a fact its diplomats emphasized during the campaign.
The withdrawal simplified the election but did not diminish the significance of the contest for the Asia-Pacific seat. Recent News –
The 81st session of the UNGA will officially open on 8 September 2026.
The high-level General Debate, where world leaders speak, will begin on Tuesday, 22 September 2026.
The session is expected to be one of the busiest in recent memory, addressing issues from sea-level rise to nuclear disarmament.
The President will also oversee the initial phase of selecting a new UN Secretary-General as Antonio Guterres's term concludes in 2027.
Both candidates have pledged to serve as "full-time presidents," bringing their extensive diplomatic experience to bear on the role.
Khalilur Rahman stated he would act "without fear or favour," serving the interests of the entire membership.
Outgoing President Annalena Baerbock used her tenure to press forward with implementation of the "Pact for the Future" and the "UN80" reforms agenda.
She delivered a wide-ranging critique of the international system's failures, invoking humanitarian suffering across the globe.
She insisted the UN still has a vital role to play, stating "Imagine how much more pain there would be without the United Nations".

topics.title: Trump’s China Visit
bullets: US President Donald Trump visited China on 13–15 May 2026 — his second visit as President and the first in his second term (which began 20 January 2025).
The summit was held in Beijing, with key meetings at the Zhongnanhai Complex — China's equivalent of the White House.
The White House originally scheduled the visit for 31 March–2 April 2026, but postponed it due to changing geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East. Background –
Trump used Section 301 of the US Trade Act (1974) to impose heavy tariffs on Chinese goods, launching the US- China trade war.
In the January 2020 Phase One Deal, China promised to buy $200 billion in US goods, while the US suspended some tariffs. However, major trade issues remained unresolved.
Trump restricted Huawei’s access to US technology and attempted to ban TikTok and WeChat, increasing technology decoupling between the two countries.
On returning to power in January 2025, Trump imposed a de facto trade embargo on China with dramatically raised tariffs.

The US retains power through advanced AI chip export controls, sanctions on Chinese purchases of Iranian oil, and the massive US consumer market China cannot ignore. Taiwan Relations Act, 1979 (USA) –
Enacted by the US Congress in 1979 after Washington formally recognised the PRC and severed official ties with Taiwan (Republic of China).
It created the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) as the unofficial diplomatic channel.

Key provisions: (1) Maintain cultural and commercial ties with Taiwan; (2) provide Taiwan with defensive arms; (3) consider any non-peaceful attempt to determine Taiwan's future a matter of 'grave concern' to the US. Past visits –
President Richard Nixon visited China from 21–28 February 1972 — the first visit by a sitting US President to the People's Republic of China.
The visit was secretly arranged by National Security Advisor Henry Kissinger, who made a covert trip to Beijing in July 1971 to lay the groundwork.
Nixon met with Chairman Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai - producing the landmark Shanghai Communiqué (1972).
President Gerald Ford visited China in December 1975 — the second US Presidential visit. Ford met Mao Zedong (in one of Mao's last foreign meetings before his death in 1976).
President Ronald Reagan visited China in April 1984 — a significant visit given Reagan's historically strong anti- Communist stance.

Reagan and Premier Zhao Ziyang signed agreements on nuclear energy cooperation and cultural exchanges. Reagan famously told Chinese students that the US was not anti-Communist but pro-freedom — causing mild diplomatic friction.

President Bill Clinton made a 9-day visit to China in June–July 1998 — the longest China visit by any US President. He met President Jiang Zemin and delivering a live televised press conference in which both leaders debated human rights openly.
Clinton's visit came just 9 years after the Tiananmen Square Massacre (June 1989) — in which the Chinese government violently cracked down on pro-democracy protests, killing hundreds to thousands.
Both sides issued a Joint Statement on Building a Constructive Strategic Partnership.

President George W. Bush visited China twice — in February 2002 and November 2005. His 2002 visit came just months after 9/11, when the US was seeking broad international support for the War on Terror.
Bush and President Jiang Zemin (2002) and later President Hu Jintao (2005) agreed on counterterrorism cooperation, trade expansion, and North Korea's nuclear programme through the Six-Party Talks.
Six-Party Talks (2003–2009) — a multilateral forum involving USA, China, Russia, Japan, South Korea, and North Korea.
President Barack Obama visited China in November 2009 (meeting President Hu Jintao) and again in November 2014 (meeting President Xi Jinping) on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in Beijing.
2009 Visit: Focused on climate change, the global financial crisis (2008 aftermath), and North Korea.

2014 Visit – Historic Climate Deal: Obama and Xi announced a landmark US-China Joint Announcement on Climate Change — the US committed to cutting emissions 26–28% below 2005 levels by 2025; China committed to peak emissions by 2030.
President Trump made a state visit to Beijing on 8–10 November 2017 — his first as President.
He was given a private tour of the Forbidden City with President Xi Jinping and a grand state banquet in the Great Hall of the People.
Trump and Xi announced $250 billion worth of trade and investment deals.
President Joe Biden (2021–2025) never made an official state visit to China However, he held multiple high-profile meetings with Xi on the sidelines of multilateral summits.
Bali Summit (November 2022): Biden and Xi met on the sidelines of the G20 in Bali, Indonesia — their first in-person meeting as presidents. Biden reaffirmed the 'One China Policy’.
San Francisco Summit (November 2023): Xi visited the US for the APEC Summit in San Francisco — meeting Biden at the Filoli Estate. UNSC –
It was established on 24th October 1945 and is headquartered in New York.
It has 15 members: 5 permanent (P5) — ➢USA, UK, France, Russia, China
Each country has veto power.
10 rotating non-permanent members (2-year terms, elected by the General Assembly).
China's P5 veto has effectively blocked any UN-endorsed military action or sanctions against Iran — allowing Iran to resist US pressure without facing a unified international response.
Article 42, UN Charter: Authorises the UNSC to take military action to maintain or restore international peace.
Article 51: Recognises the right to self-defence. Both articles are central to the legal debate over the Iran War's legitimacy. JCPOA –
Signed on 14 July 2015 between Iran and the P5+1 (USA, UK, France, Russia, China + Germany) plus the European Union.
Key terms - Iran limits uranium enrichment to 3.67%, reduces enriched uranium stockpile to 300 kg, allows IAEA inspections in exchange for lifting of international economic sanctions.
In 2018, during his first term, Trump withdrew from the JCPOA, called it the “worst deal ever negotiated,” and reimposed sanctions. Iran later increased uranium enrichment to 60%. WTO –
The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established on 1 January 1995 as the successor to GATT (1947). Both the US and China are members.
Section 301, US Trade Act (1974): Allows the US President to impose trade sanctions on countries found to engage in unfair trade practices, IP theft, or market distortion.
The proposed 'Board of Trade' between the US and China discussed at the summit would be a bilateral non-WTO mechanism for resolving disputes. Recent Visit –
Xi Jinping welcomed Trump at the Great Hall of the People, where both leaders held official talks.
After the meeting, they visited the Temple of Heaven, making Trump only the second sitting US President after Gerald Ford in 1975 to visit the site.
Xi later hosted a state banquet for Trump at the Great Hall of the People, and Trump invited Xi for a future state visit to the United States on 24th September 2026.
Trump was joined by top US corporate leaders – Musk, Cook, Huang, Fink, Ortberg – signaling a focus on investment and tech cooperation and Xi personally met them.
Unlike the other CEOs, Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Elon Musk (Tesla/SpaceX) directly travelled with Trump on Air Force One.
The delegation highlights mutual economic dependency: US tech firms rely on Chinese supply chains and markets, while China depends on US technology, investment, and agricultural imports.
